question: Which state statute is the primary source of Pennsylvania's housing antidiscrimination law, referenced directly in RELRA Section 604(22)?
choice_a: The Pennsylvania Fair Housing Act of 1988
choice_b: The Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, act of October 27, 1955, P.L. 744, No. 222
choice_c: The Real Estate Licensing and Registration Act itself, with no separate housing-discrimination statute
choice_d: Title VIII of the federal Civil Rights Act of 1968 alone, with no state analog
explanation: RELRA Section 604(22) expressly cross-references 'the act of October 27, 1955 (P.L.744, No.222), known as the "Pennsylvania Human Relations Act,"' making a violation (or a PHRC order/consent decree arising from one) tied to real-estate activities an independently disciplinable RELRA violation.
source_note: 63 P.S. Section 455.604(22); Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, 43 P.S. Sections 951-963 (both confirmed verbatim via legis.state.pa.us)

question: Which protected classes are listed under RELRA Section 604(22)(i) as bases on which a licensee may not accept discriminatory listings or give false discriminatory information?
choice_a: Only race and color, with all other categories left to federal law exclusively
choice_b: Political party affiliation and religious creed only
choice_c: Race, color, religious creed, sex, ancestry, national origin, physical handicap, disability, or use of a guide dog because of blindness
choice_d: Marital status is the only protected category listed
explanation: RELRA Section 604(22)(i)(A)-(C) specifically lists race, color, religious creed, sex, ancestry, national origin, physical handicap, disability, or use of a guide dog because of blindness as the protected categories relevant to accepting discriminatory listings, giving false information for discriminatory purposes, or making discriminatory distinctions in housing availability.

question: Under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, which protected classes appear at 43 P.S. Section 955(h) for housing discrimination that are NOT explicitly listed among RELRA Section 604(22)'s enumerated categories?
explanation: The PHRA's housing-discrimination section, 43 P.S. Section 955(h), reaches age and familial status among its protected classes, broadening coverage beyond the narrower list directly enumerated in RELRA Section 604(22)(i) -- a useful illustration of how the PHRA (the substantive discrimination statute) and RELRA (the licensing-discipline statute cross-referencing it) work together.
source_note: 43 P.S. Section 955(h)(1)-(11) (confirmed via research pass on PHRA housing provisions); 63 P.S. Section 455.604(22)(i) (confirmed) -- comparison is this project's own synthesis of the two statutes' respective protected-class lists

question: What real estate practice does PHRA Section 955.3 ('Prohibition of Certain Real Estate Practices') specifically target?
choice_a: Blockbusting/panic-peddling -- inducing or soliciting a listing, sale, or transaction for commercial profit by representing that a protected class is moving into or is present in a neighborhood
choice_b: Charging different commission rates to different clients
choice_c: Refusing to cooperate with the local multiple listing service
choice_d: Requiring a home inspection before closing
explanation: PHRA Section 955.3 targets blockbusting: it is unlawful for any person to induce, solicit, or attempt to induce or solicit for commercial profit any listing, sale, or transaction involving housing by representing that the property is within, or adjacent to, an area where persons of a particular protected class reside -- a practice that exploits racial or other prejudice to churn transactions.
source_note: 43 P.S. Section 955.3 (confirmed via research pass citing the PHRA's real estate practices provisions and its cross-reference in 49 Pa. Code regulatory authority notes)

question: If a licensee is accused of a SECOND or subsequent housing-discrimination complaint, does the 90-day PHRC-first waiting period of RELRA Section 604(22)(iii) still apply?
choice_a: Yes -- every complaint against the same licensee triggers a fresh 90-day PHRC-first period
choice_b: No -- the 90-day waiting period applies only to a licensee's initial complaint; second or subsequent complaints may go directly to the State Real Estate Commission
choice_c: No -- after a second complaint, the PHRC loses jurisdiction over the matter entirely
choice_d: The rule applies only to complaints filed by the same complainant twice
explanation: RELRA Section 604(22)(iv) expressly limits the 90-day PHRC head-start to a licensee's INITIAL discrimination complaint; second or subsequent complaints may be brought directly to the State Real Estate Commission by individuals or the PHRC itself, without waiting.

question: May the State Real Estate Commission conduct its own independent investigation of a discrimination complaint while the PHRC is also investigating the same matter?
choice_a: No -- only one agency may investigate a given complaint at a time
choice_b: Yes, but only after obtaining a court order permitting parallel investigation
choice_c: Yes -- RELRA Section 604(22)(ii) states nothing precludes the Commission from conducting its own investigation and maintaining its own file
choice_d: No -- the PHRC has exclusive jurisdiction over all discrimination complaints against real estate licensees
explanation: RELRA Section 604(22)(ii) clarifies that nothing in the paragraph precludes the State Real Estate Commission from conducting its own investigation and maintaining its own file on a discrimination complaint -- the 90-day rule governs the timing of Commission ACTION (discipline), not investigation.

question: Under the national portion of the Pearson VUE broker exam content outline, fair housing content within 'Real Estate Practice' covers which specific federal agency and law by name?
choice_a: The Federal Trade Commission and the Sherman Antitrust Act only
choice_b: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau exclusively
choice_c: The Department of Justice's Civil Rights Division only
choice_d: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
explanation: The Pearson VUE national broker content outline's Real Estate Practice section (Item V.C, 'Fair Housing') lists equal opportunity in housing, protected classes, fair housing laws, illegal practices/enforcement/penalties, prohibited advertising, HUD, and the ADA as the specific tested subtopics.
source_note: Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers, effective April 1, 2025 (confirmed directly from the official candidate handbook PDF via pdftotext)

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as amended), which of these is a federally protected class not always explicitly named in every state fair housing statute enacted before the 1988 amendments?
choice_a: Familial status and disability (handicap), added by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
choice_b: Race, which was first added only in 1988
choice_c: Religion, which the federal act has never covered
choice_d: Color, which is not a federally protected class
explanation: The original 1968 federal Fair Housing Act covered race, color, religion, and national origin; sex was added in 1974; familial status and disability (handicap) were added by the Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 -- a standard, well-corroborated federal fair-housing history point tested on the national portion of nearly every state's broker exam.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal fair housing law history (42 U.S.C. Section 3601 et seq. and its 1988 amendments), not a Pennsylvania-specific citation

question: Under federal fair housing law, does the exemption for owner-occupied buildings with a limited number of units ('Mrs. Murphy' exemption) ever apply to a transaction handled by a licensed real estate broker?
choice_a: Yes, without limitation, regardless of broker involvement
choice_b: No -- the Mrs. Murphy exemption is generally understood to be lost once a licensed real estate broker or agent is used to arrange the transaction, even if the property would otherwise qualify
choice_c: The exemption applies only to commercial property, never residential
choice_d: The exemption was repealed nationwide in 1988 and no longer exists in any form
explanation: The federal Fair Housing Act's limited exemptions for certain owner-occupied small buildings and single-family homes sold/rented without a broker are widely understood in real estate education to be forfeited once a licensed broker or agent, or discriminatory advertising, is used -- a standard national-content-outline point rather than a PA-specific statutory citation.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated federal Fair Housing Act exemption doctrine, not independently pinpoint-verified against a specific PA statute in this research pass

question: May a broker refuse to show a listed property to a prospective buyer because of the buyer's use of a guide dog due to blindness?
choice_a: Yes, if the seller specifically requests it in the listing agreement
choice_b: Yes, as long as the refusal is not communicated in writing
choice_c: No -- RELRA Section 604(22)(i) specifically lists 'use of a guide dog because of blindness' among the bases on which discriminatory conduct is disciplinable
choice_d: This scenario is not addressed anywhere in Pennsylvania real estate law
explanation: RELRA Section 604(22)(i)(A)-(C) repeatedly lists 'use of a guide dog because of blindness of user' alongside race, color, religious creed, sex, ancestry, national origin, physical handicap, and disability as protected categories for purposes of accepting listings, giving information, or making distinctions in housing availability.

question: Within how many days of an alleged act of housing discrimination must a complaint generally be filed with the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission (PHRC)?
explanation: The PHRC's own filing guidance states a complaint generally must be filed within 180 days of the alleged discriminatory act, unless the complainant shows legal justification for a delay -- notably shorter than the 1-year deadline available for a parallel complaint filed with HUD under federal fair housing law.
source_note: PHRC 'File a Complaint' guidance, pa.gov (confirmed via research pass on PHRC filing deadlines)

question: Does the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act recognize a broad 'Mrs. Murphy'-style exemption allowing an owner to discriminate freely in any small owner-occupied rental building?
choice_a: No -- Pennsylvania's exemption is narrower, applying only to a building with just TWO units where the owner occupies one of them as a primary residence
choice_b: Yes -- any building with up to four units qualifies for the exemption, regardless of owner-occupancy
choice_c: Yes -- the exemption applies to any rental property regardless of size, as long as no broker is involved
choice_d: No exemption of any kind exists for owner-occupied rental property in Pennsylvania
explanation: Pennsylvania's PHRA exemption is notably narrower than the federal Fair Housing Act's owner-occupied exemption: it applies only to a two-unit building where the owner occupies one unit as a primary residence and personally chooses who lives in the other unit -- larger owner-occupied buildings, or buildings not personally occupied by the owner, do not qualify.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated secondary sources (landlord/tenant fair-housing advocacy organizations) describing the PHRA's narrow two-unit owner-occupied exemption at 43 P.S. Section 955(h); exact statutory subsection not independently pinpoint-verified against primary legislative text in this research pass

question: May a religious organization operating housing limit occupancy to its own members without violating the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act?
choice_a: No -- religious organizations have no exemption whatsoever under the PHRA
choice_b: Yes -- housing operated by religious organizations (and private clubs) may limit occupancy to members, so long as membership itself is not restricted on a discriminatory basis
choice_c: Yes, without any limitation, even if membership itself is restricted by race
choice_d: This exemption applies only to for-profit religious-affiliated developers
explanation: The PHRA (consistent with the parallel federal Fair Housing Act religious-organization exemption) allows housing operated by a bona fide religious organization or private club to prefer its own members, provided membership in that organization is not itself restricted on a discriminatory basis (e.g., by race).
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated secondary sources on PHRA/federal Fair Housing Act religious-organization exemptions; exact PHRA subsection not independently pinpoint-verified against primary legislative text in this research pass

question: Which categories of housing discrimination complaint does the PHRA cover, per PHRC's own guidance?
choice_a: Only discrimination occurring during the actual closing/settlement process
choice_b: Only discrimination by licensed real estate brokers, not by lenders or sellers directly
choice_c: Discrimination in the renting, buying, selling, or financing (obtaining a loan for) a home
choice_d: Only discrimination in commercial (non-residential) property transactions
explanation: The PHRC's guidance confirms housing discrimination under the PHRA can occur throughout the process of renting, buying, selling, or obtaining financing for a home -- covering lenders and private sellers, not merely licensed real estate brokers and salespersons.
source_note: PHRC housing discrimination guidance, pa.gov (confirmed via research pass)

question: Is 'source of income' (e.g., a Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher) a protected class under statewide Pennsylvania law (the PHRA)?
choice_a: Yes -- source of income has been a statewide PHRA protected class since the Act's original 1955 enactment
choice_b: Yes -- source of income is protected under the federal Fair Housing Act nationwide
choice_c: No jurisdiction in Pennsylvania protects source of income in any way
choice_d: No -- source of income is not a protected class under the statewide PHRA or federal fair housing law; it is protected only where a LOCAL ordinance separately provides for it, such as Philadelphia's Fair Practices Ordinance
explanation: Source of income (including rental assistance/housing vouchers) is NOT a protected class under Pennsylvania's statewide PHRA or under federal fair housing law -- that protection exists only where a local ordinance creates it, notably Philadelphia's Fair Practices Ordinance (Philadelphia Code Section 9-1100 et seq.), which bars discrimination based on 'source of lawful income,' including housing assistance programs/vouchers, within city limits.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated secondary sources (equalhousing.org, Reed Smith LLP legal analysis) confirming source of income is a LOCAL Philadelphia protection, not a statewide PHRA protected class; Philadelphia Code Section 9-1100 et seq. confirmed via research pass, though PA's approach on this specific point is genuinely a patchwork by municipality rather than a single statewide rule

question: A licensee working in Philadelphia refuses to rent an apartment to a prospective tenant solely because the tenant intends to pay using a Section 8 housing voucher. Under Philadelphia's local Fair Practices Ordinance, what type of relief could a successful complainant obtain?
choice_a: A cease-and-desist order, injunctive/equitable relief, compensatory or punitive damages, and attorneys' fees
choice_b: No remedy exists because source-of-income discrimination is entirely legal statewide
choice_c: Only a formal written warning, with no monetary remedy available
choice_d: Automatic revocation of the landlord's business license, with no other remedy option
explanation: Philadelphia's Fair Practices Ordinance provides for a range of remedies in a source-of-income discrimination case, including a cease-and-desist order, injunctive or equitable relief, compensatory or punitive damages, and recovery of attorneys' fees and other expenses -- illustrating that even where a protection is purely local (not statewide), it can carry real remedial consequences for licensees operating within that municipality.
